title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) we ran N = 300 matched intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) in a Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator using a declared model (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM candidate replayed to both arms to conserve provider calls). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no validator reported forbidden reachability and no repair was invoked, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about verifier-guided repair efficacy was untestable in this run. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on the undetected baseline violation rate. The empirical contribution is deterministic execution accounting, artifact-backed contingency statistics, and artifact-grounded design lessons (generation semantics, adversary strength, repair budget, and verifier diversity) to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the study evidence bundle to enable independent verification.

sections.introduction: LLMs promise automation for intent-driven network configuration, but operators are justifiably concerned that generated artifacts can expand attack surface or violate policy. Prior systems and surveys therefore recommend constrained generation, execution oracles, or generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations. We sought a narrowly scoped, preregistered confirmatory test: does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM intent→configuration pipeline? We implemented a paired N = 300 design and deterministic execution under a frozen protocol (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). Key contributions: (1) a preregistered, deterministic paired execution with complete per-episode validator traces and provider-call accounting; (2) a concise, artifact-grounded quantitative result (n11 = 300, no repairs invoked) and derived bounds on undetected baseline violation rate; (3) an explicit statement that the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy was untestable here due to shared_initial_candidate generation semantics combined with zero observed baseline violations; and (4) artifact-grounded operational recommendations for follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair path.
sections.related_work: Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness in code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to drive repair; system examples demonstrate verifier-in-the-loop gains but vary by verifier and repair strategy [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight for operational use [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Emulation and testbed studies show execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation but warn of external-validity gaps to production devices [https://openalex.org/W4406170828]. The supplied literature set contains limited prior demonstrations of preregistered, verifier-in-the-loop confirmatory evaluations for security-relevant predicates, motivating the present artifact-centered study.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05) on complete matched pairs. Sampling, deduplication (exact duplicates and fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15), exclusions, and sensitivity rules were fixed in the preregistration. Adapter contract and generation semantics: to limit model-call cost the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each pair a single initial LLM candidate was generated and that same candidate was replayed to both arms (baseline; guarded). This choice produced model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs instead of up to 600 for independent draws. Intervention arms: Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded = same candidate validated by deterministic validators; if any validator flagged the forbidden-reachability predicate, the pipeline was allowed up to one repair LLM call per pair (repair policy preregistered). Validators and forbidden-reachability predicate (concise technical definition): the forbidden-reachability predicate reports whether any policy-protected source→destination pair becomes reachable under the generated configuration (a policy-violation reachability event). Two deterministic validators implemented the predicate: (i) a containerized Batfish-style execution validator that deterministically simulates device configuration semantics in the emulated environment, and (ii) a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer implemented in Python. Validators were combined with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair was labeled violating if any validator reported forbidden reachability. Execution environment and reproducibility: the environment used Dockerized FRRouting-style router images and deterministic orchestration; seeds, task manifests, per-episode raw responses, per-episode validator traces, and provider-call audit are archived in the evidence bundle. Analysis plan: primary inference used McNemar on complete matched pairs; prespecified bootstrap percentile CIs (preregistered 1,000 resamples) were computed; final analysis used 10,000 resamples with bootstrap_seed = 1729 (recorded in analysis log) to reduce Monte Carlo error. Sensitivity analyses for missingness and contamination were preregistered; no technical failures occurred.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0. Provider-call accounting under the shared_initial_candidate contract: model_calls_used = 300 (maximum_model_calls allowed by contract = 600). Primary confirmatory outcome: all 300 complete pairs passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency table: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired risk-difference (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no validator ever reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate, no repair call was invoked (all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false) and verifier_disagreement_rate = 0. Interpretation of degenerate contingency: with zero discordant pairs the paired test is uninformative about repair efficacy—the design produced no opportunities for repair to act. Descriptive bound: observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the true baseline violation probability of approximately 0.00994 (≈0.994%). Representative artifacts: per-episode examples (responses and validator traces) are archived to permit spot-checking of parsing, normalization, and validator judgments; the most important artifacts are archived under the study evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration ID.
sections.discussion: What the evidence supports: under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), validator set (two deterministic validators combined by logical OR), emulator, and programmatic adversarial variants used here, baseline generation was compliant with the forbidden-reachability predicate on all sampled intents; thus inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archived provider-call accounting, per-episode validator traces, and contingency statistics consistently record that no forbidden-reachability events were detected. What the evidence does not show: because the repair path was never invoked, this experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy was therefore untestable in this run. Design lessons (artifact-grounded): (1) Generation semantics matter—shared_initial_candidate reduces model calls but also reduces independent-sample variability needed to elicit discordant violating outputs; to exercise repair efficacy use independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or expand repair budgets. (2) Adversary potency matters—the programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators; stronger or targeted adversaries are needed to stress verifiers. (3) Verifier diversity and strength matter—combining multiple oracle families (execution, control-plane, data-plane, or production-grade oracles) increases chance of detecting realistic violations. (4) Reproducibility is practical—complete per-episode traces and provider-call audits are archived to support exact replay and targeted stress tests. Threats to validity: internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope; construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately capture operational security risk; external validity is limited by synthetic tasks and Dockerized emulation; conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and the preregistered power assumptions are not met. These limitations are artifact-referenced to support transparent reanalysis.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation using a declared model (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators (Batfish-style execution and a graph-based static reachability analyzer), and a shared_initial_candidate contract. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms were compliant on all pairs (n11 = 300), no repairs were invoked, McNemar p = 1.0, and the bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because the repair path was not exercised, the experiment cannot answer whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations; instead it quantifies that, under the chosen contract and artifacts, baseline generation was compliant on the sampled intents and bounds the undetected baseline violation rate (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to inform follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render the McNemar test uninformative about repair efficacy; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: validators never reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
